title: Spacesuits: Protection in the Void
summary: How a spacesuit's layers supply oxygen, hold pressure, control temperature, and shield an astronaut from radiation and micrometeoroids during a spacewalk.
poll: A spacesuit is really just a tiny personal spacecraft.

versions.title: A Suit for Space
versions.text:
Space has no air. It is a vacuum. No one can breathe there.

A person wears a suit to go in space. The suit holds air. It has oxygen to breathe.

The suit has a hard helmet. It has a clear visor. A person can see out of it. It blocks bright light.

The suit has thick gloves too. They let a person use their hands. They keep hands safe and warm.

Space can get very hot. It can get very cold too. The suit keeps the body at a safe heat.

Without a suit, a person could not live in space. The suit is like a tiny home.

versions.title: Spacesuits: Protection in the Void
versions.text:
Space has no air at all. Scientists call this a vacuum. A person cannot breathe there. Without a suit, a person could not live for even a short time.

To stay alive, an astronaut wears a special suit. The suit holds air around the body. It carries its own oxygen to breathe. The suit protects the astronaut from danger.

The suit also has a hard helmet. At the front is a clear visor. The astronaut looks through it. It blocks the Sun's bright light.

Thick gloves cover the hands. They let the astronaut grip tools. They keep fingers safe and warm. The gloves still let the astronaut move each finger.

In space, the heat swings between very hot and very cold. One side can be burning hot. The other side can be freezing cold. The suit works to keep the body safe.

Without a suit, an astronaut could not survive even a few seconds in space. A suit is like a tiny spacecraft worn by a person.

versions.title: Spacesuits: Protection in the Void
versions.text:
Space has no air at all. Scientists call this a vacuum. A person cannot breathe there. Without a suit, a person could not live for even a short time.

To stay alive, an astronaut wears a special suit. It is built from several layers. The suit holds air around the body. It carries its own oxygen to breathe.

The suit also has a hard helmet. At the front is a clear visor. The visor has a thin layer of gold on it. The astronaut looks through it. It blocks the Sun's bright light.

Thick, padded gloves cover the hands. Even though they are thick, they still let the astronaut grip tools firmly. They keep fingers safe and warm.

In space, the heat swings between very hot and very cold. One side can be burning hot. The other side can be freezing cold. The suit works hard to keep the body safe no matter which side faces the Sun.

Without a suit, an astronaut could not survive even a few seconds in the vacuum of space. A suit is like a tiny spacecraft worn by a person.

versions.title: Spacesuits: Protection in the Void
versions.text:
Outside a spacecraft, space is a true vacuum. There is no air at all. It is also full of harmful radiation from the Sun and from deep space. Because of this, no person could survive there without protection. To survive, astronauts depend on their spacesuits.

A modern suit is built in several layers. Next to the skin is a thin garment with tubes of cooling water. These tubes carry away body heat during hard work. Around that is a tough, airtight layer. It keeps the suit under steady pressure, much like the air inside an airplane.

Over the pressure layer is a thick layer of insulation. It shields the astronaut from extreme heat and cold, and from tiny flying debris. The helmet's gold visor also blocks the Sun's radiation and glare.

A backpack called the life support system rides on the back. It supplies oxygen to breathe. It removes the carbon dioxide breathed out. It keeps the suit running during a spacewalk, when an astronaut leaves the spacecraft to work in open space.

Every part of the suit works together. Engineers design each layer so an astronaut can work safely far from home. This teamwork lets an astronaut survive during a spacewalk.

versions.title: Spacesuits: Engineering Survival in the Vacuum of Space
versions.text:
The environment beyond a spacecraft's hull is a true and total vacuum containing no air whatsoever. It is also constantly full of harmful radiation streaming from the Sun and from deep outer space. Because of this, no person could survive direct exposure there without protection. Astronauts depend entirely on their specially engineered spacesuits, formally called extravehicular mobility units. Engineers designed these suits specifically to handle such extreme and hostile conditions. Even a tiny gap in a suit's seal could put an astronaut's life at risk. Space also has almost no pressure at all, unlike the air here on Earth.

A modern suit is carefully built in several distinct layers, each with its own purpose. Next to the skin is a thin liquid cooling and ventilation garment with narrow tubes of circulating cooling water that carry away body heat during long periods of hard physical work. Around that is a tough, airtight pressure layer that must regulate internal pressure carefully, much like the air pressure inside an airplane cabin.

Over the pressure layer is a thick outer layer of insulation and protective fabric, built to guard against micrometeoroids, tiny particles of rock or debris that travel fast enough to puncture unprotected material. The helmet's gold-coated visor also regulates how much of the Sun's dangerous radiation and blinding glare reaches the astronaut's eyes.

A backpack known as the life support system rides securely on the back. It continuously regulates oxygen supply and removes the carbon dioxide breathed out. Without this backpack, an astronaut could not stay outside for very long. It keeps the whole suit running properly throughout extravehicular activity, commonly called a spacewalk.

Every single part of the suit must work together flawlessly. Engineers carefully design each layer so an astronaut can work safely far from home, and this teamwork lets an astronaut survive during each demanding spacewalk.

versions.title: Spacesuits: Engineering Survival in the Vacuum of Space
versions.text:
The environment beyond a spacecraft's hull is a profoundly and relentlessly hostile vacuum containing no air whatsoever, and it is also constantly and mercilessly bombarded by intense radiation streaming from the Sun and from deep outer space, conditions that would prove fatal to any unprotected human within mere moments. Because of this, no person could survive direct exposure there without protection, so astronauts depend entirely on their specially and painstakingly engineered spacesuits, formally termed extravehicular mobility units, which engineers designed specifically to counter such extreme and hostile conditions. Space also has almost no pressure at all, unlike the air here on Earth, and astronauts must prepare meticulously for every single one of these dangers before each demanding mission.

A modern suit is meticulously built in several distinct layers, each with its own essential purpose. Next to the skin is a thin liquid cooling and ventilation garment with narrow tubing of circulating cooling water that carries away body heat during long periods of strenuous physical exertion, while surrounding that is a tough, airtight pressure layer that must continuously and precisely regulate internal pressure, much like the carefully maintained air pressure inside an airplane cabin.

Over the pressure layer is a thick outer layer of insulation and protective fabric, built to guard against micrometeoroids, tiny particles of rock or orbital debris that travel at tremendous velocities fast enough to puncture unprotected material almost instantaneously upon impact. These particles move through space at incredible speeds, so even a very small one can cause catastrophic damage. The helmet's gold-coated visor also precisely regulates exactly how much of the Sun's dangerous radiation and blinding glare ultimately reaches the astronaut's eyes.

A backpack known as the portable life support system rides securely on the back, continuously regulating the astronaut's oxygen supply while tirelessly removing the carbon dioxide breathed out, and this system also communicates constantly with mission control back on Earth. Engineers carefully design each layer so an astronaut can work safely far from home, and this teamwork lets an astronaut survive during each demanding spacewalk.

From the carefully regulated pressure layer that keeps an astronaut's body safe, to the outer shielding that turns aside micrometeoroids and radiation alike, every single component of a spacesuit exists for one unforgiving reason: without it, exposure to the vacuum of space would be fatal within seconds, and no astronaut could ever safely leave the shelter of their spacecraft to begin extravehicular activity.

keyWords.definition: a very tiny piece of rock or space debris that can travel fast enough to damage a spacecraft or suit
keyWords.example: A micrometeoroid left a small dent in the side of the space station.

keyWords.definition: the movement of air or fluid through a space to control temperature or supply fresh air
keyWords.example: Good ventilation in the tunnel kept the air from getting too stale.
The crew prepared carefully before their extravehicular activity outside the station.

keyWords.definition: the condition of being unprotected against something harmful, such as extreme cold or radiation
keyWords.example: Hikers wore heavy coats to avoid exposure to the freezing wind.

keyWords.definition: to control something so that it stays steady or within safe limits
keyWords.example: A thermostat helps regulate the temperature inside a house.

questions.stem: What is the central idea of the article?
options: Engineers have never successfully tested a spacesuit, so astronauts must work outside with only simple clothing and no air.
A spacesuit combines cooling, pressure, insulation, and radiation shielding into one system engineered to let an astronaut survive extravehicular activity.
Micrometeoroids are not a real danger in space, so a spacesuit needs no outer layers and can be made as thin as a shirt.
The ventilation garment is the only part of a spacesuit that matters, because the other layers, the helmet and the gloves, are never used by astronauts.
questions.why: The article connects cooling, pressure regulation, insulation, and radiation shielding as the systems that let an astronaut survive extravehicular activity.

wrong.A: The article says engineers test suits extensively, implying successful testing.
wrong.C: The article describes micrometeoroids as a real danger that the suit protects against.
wrong.D: The article describes several equally important layers, not just the ventilation garment.

questions.stem: According to the article, what is the formal name for a spacesuit?
options: An extravehicular mobility unit
A particular kind of pressure capsule used only indoors
A specific kind of ventilation module for spacecraft
A specialized thermal backpack worn under the suit
questions.why: In the article, a spacesuit is formally termed an extravehicular mobility unit.

wrong.B: A pressure capsule is not the name given in the article.
wrong.C: A ventilation module is not the formal name used.
wrong.D: A thermal backpack is not the term the article uses.

questions.stem: What does the liquid cooling and ventilation garment do?
options: It blocks harmful radiation coming from the Sun
It supplies fresh oxygen for the astronaut to breathe
It carries away body heat using circulating water
It protects the suit against tiny micrometeoroids outside
questions.why: In the article, the liquid cooling and ventilation garment circulates water through tubes to carry away body heat.

wrong.A: Blocking radiation is the visor's job, not the cooling garment's.
wrong.B: The backpack supplies oxygen, not the cooling garment.
wrong.D: The outer garment protects against micrometeoroids, not the cooling garment.

questions.stem: Why must the pressure layer regulate internal pressure so carefully?
options: To make the suit lighter for the astronaut to carry during a long walk outside
To help the visor block more sunlight and glare from the Sun on the dusty ground
To let the backpack supply more oxygen to the astronaut's helmet for a longer time
Because the unprotected human body cannot survive direct exposure to the vacuum of space
questions.why: The article explains that the unprotected human body cannot survive direct exposure to the vacuum of space, so pressure must be carefully regulated.

wrong.A: Weight is not the reason given for regulating pressure.
wrong.B: The visor's sunlight blocking is unrelated to pressure regulation.
wrong.C: Oxygen supply is handled by the backpack, not the pressure layer.

questions.stem: In the article, what are micrometeoroids?
options: Tiny particles of rock or debris that can puncture material
A particular kind of harmful solar radiation reaching Earth
A specific layer found inside the pressure garment itself
A specialized tool used only to repair broken spacesuits
questions.why: The article defines micrometeoroids as tiny particles of rock or debris traveling fast enough to puncture unprotected material.

wrong.B: Solar radiation is a separate hazard from micrometeoroids.
wrong.C: A layer of the suit is not what micrometeoroid means.
wrong.D: A repair tool is not mentioned as a micrometeoroid.

questions.stem: Based on the article, how is the outer thermal and micrometeoroid garment different from the inner cooling and ventilation garment?
options: The outer garment supplies oxygen to the astronaut, while the inner garment does not
The inner garment blocks radiation, while the outer garment carries water to the body
The outer garment resists temperature swings and debris; the inner one removes body heat
The two garments perform exactly the same identical job in the suit, with no difference
questions.why: The article explains that the outer garment provides insulation and protects against micrometeoroids, while the inner garment carries away body heat through circulating water.

wrong.A: Oxygen supply comes from the backpack, not either garment.
wrong.B: The article says the outer layer protects against temperature and debris, and the inner layer handles cooling, not radiation.
wrong.D: The two garments serve different purposes.

questions.stem: What can be inferred about why engineers test each spacesuit many times before it protects an astronaut?
options: Testing is required mostly for appearance, so that the spacesuit looks bright and clean in photos and videos on Earth
Spacesuits rarely function correctly on the first attempt, so engineers must try again and again
Testing is unrelated to astronaut safety, because the suits are already made by machines
Because every layer must work correctly at once, a single failure could expose the astronaut to a fatal environment
questions.why: The article explains that because every layer must function correctly at once, extensive testing helps prevent a failure that could expose the astronaut to a fatal environment.

wrong.A: Appearance is not mentioned as a reason for testing.
wrong.B: The article does not say suits rarely work; it says testing confirms they will.
wrong.C: The article directly connects testing to astronaut safety.

questions.stem: Why does the author describe the suit from the innermost layer outward to the backpack?
options: To argue that outer layers matter more than inner ones, because they meet the cold and dust first
To help readers understand how each layer builds on the one before it to protect the astronaut
To compare the suit with ordinary clothing that children wear in school or at home
To list every astronaut who has worn a spacesuit, from the first to the most recent
questions.why: Describing the suit from the inner layer outward helps readers see how each layer adds its own protection to the one before it.

wrong.A: The article presents all layers as working together, not one mattering more.
wrong.C: Ordinary clothing is not compared in the article.
wrong.D: No list of astronauts appears in the article.

HIGH.prompt: Explain how the pressure layer and the thermal and micrometeoroid garment work together to protect an astronaut during extravehicular activity. Use details from the article.
checklist: I explained what the pressure layer regulates.
I explained what the micrometeoroid garment protects against.
I used precise words such as extravehicular, ventilation, and exposure.
HIGH.modelAnswer: The pressure layer is an airtight garment that must continuously regulate internal pressure, because the unprotected human body cannot survive direct exposure to the vacuum of space. Surrounding that layer, the outer thermal and micrometeoroid garment adds insulation against extreme temperature swings and protects against micrometeoroids, the tiny, fast-moving particles of rock or debris that could otherwise puncture the suit. Together, the regulated pressure layer and the protective outer garment let an astronaut safely undertake extravehicular activity, since losing either layer's protection could quickly turn a routine spacewalk into a life-threatening emergency.

LOW.stem: What do the thick gloves let a person do?
options: Fly through space fast
See in the dark
Use their hands
Hear sounds clearly
LOW.why: In the text, the thick gloves let a person use their hands.

wrong.A: The text does not say gloves help a person fly.
wrong.B: Gloves are not linked to seeing in the dark.
wrong.D: Gloves are not linked to hearing.

LOW.stem: Why does the suit need to keep the body at a safe heat?
options: Space can be very hot and very cold
Space is always the same warm heat
The helmet gets too heavy to hold
The gloves are made of thick metal
LOW.why: In the text, space can get very hot and very cold, so the suit keeps the body at a safe heat.

wrong.B: The text says space changes from hot to cold.
wrong.C: Weight of the helmet is not the reason given.
wrong.D: The text does not say the gloves are made of metal.

LOW.stem: The text says it blocks bright light. What does blocks mean here?
options: Lets in more of
Makes much louder
Paints bright colors on
Stops from getting through
LOW.why: The visor keeps bright light out so the person can see.

wrong.A: The visor protects the eyes, so it does not let more light in.
wrong.B: The sentence is about light, not sound.
wrong.C: Nothing is painted on the visor.

LOW.stem: What is the last paragraph mostly about?
options: How to make a new space helmet at home
Why a suit is needed to live in space
Where to buy a space suit for a trip
How gloves keep hands safe and warm
LOW.why: It says that without a suit a person could not live in space, and that the suit is like a tiny home.

wrong.A: The paragraph does not talk about making a helmet.
wrong.C: Buying suits is never mentioned.
wrong.D: Gloves are in an earlier paragraph.

MID.stem: What harmful thing from the Sun and deep space fills space?
options: Radiation
Heavy rain
Strong wind
Thick smoke
MID.why: The text says space is full of harmful radiation from the Sun and from deep space.

wrong.B: Space has no rain.
wrong.C: Space has no air, so it has no wind.
wrong.D: The text does not mention smoke.

MID.stem: Why does the suit have tubes of cooling water next to the skin?
options: To help the astronaut float around
To keep the helmet clean and clear
To carry away body heat during hard work
To make the suit look bright and shiny
MID.why: The text says the tubes carry away body heat during hard work.

wrong.A: Floating is not linked to the water tubes.
wrong.B: The tubes are not about the helmet.
wrong.D: Looks are not mentioned.

MID.stem: Read: "a tough, airtight layer." What does airtight most likely mean?
options: Made of thin cloth
Full of cold water
Made to be very light
Letting no air in or out
MID.why: This layer keeps the suit under steady pressure, so air must not get in or out.

wrong.A: The layer is described as tough, not thin.
wrong.B: The water tubes are in a different layer.
wrong.C: Weight is not the point of the word.

MID.stem: What does the backpack remove from the air inside the suit?
options: Oxygen
Carbon dioxide
Water
Heat
MID.why: In the text, the backpack removes the carbon dioxide breathed out.

wrong.A: The backpack supplies oxygen, it does not remove it.
wrong.C: Water is used in the cooling tubes.
wrong.D: Cooling is done by the tubes, not by removing air.

HIGH.stem: What is the commonly used name for "extravehicular activity"?
options: A launch
A landing
A spacewalk
A docking
HIGH.why: The text says extravehicular activity is commonly called a spacewalk.

wrong.A: A launch is the start of a flight.
wrong.B: A landing is the end of a flight.
wrong.D: Docking is joining two spacecraft.

HIGH.stem: Read: "extreme and hostile conditions." What does hostile mean here?
options: Dangerous and unfriendly
Warm and welcoming
Quiet and calm
Bright and colorful
HIGH.why: Space has no air and harmful radiation, so its conditions are dangerous.

wrong.B: Welcoming is the opposite of the text.
wrong.C: Space is not described as calm.
wrong.D: Colors are not the point of the sentence.

HIGH.stem: Why could even a tiny gap in a suit's seal put an astronaut's life at risk?
options: The suit would become too heavy
The astronaut would lose the visor
The cooling water would turn to ice
Space has almost no pressure or air
HIGH.why: In the text, space has almost no pressure and no air, so a gap would let the suit's air out.

wrong.A: Weight is not the problem.
wrong.B: The visor is not linked to the seal.
wrong.C: The text does not say the water would freeze.

HIGH.stem: Why do engineers test the suit's backpack many times?
options: So it never fails during a mission
So it looks bright in space
So it can be sold after the mission
So it becomes lighter each time
HIGH.why: Engineers test the backpack many times to make sure it never fails, because an astronaut needs it to stay outside.

wrong.B: Color is not the reason for testing.
wrong.C: Selling the backpack is not mentioned.
wrong.D: Testing does not make it lighter.
